doom.driver: Kenya confirms its first Ebola death as outbreak spreads. The patient had been living in DR Congo, where more than 4,000 people have died from the disease this year.
doom.blurb: 4,000 DEAD, NOW PLAYING AWAY IN KENYA
doom.summary: Ebola just crossed a border with 28 contacts in tow, while the DRC toll tops 4,000. Meanwhile, nearly 20 tankers have been hit around Hormuz in a month, drones are sinking ships in the Black Sea, and Lithuania wants nuclear weapons back on the menu. Add OpenAI agents going 'rogue' on Wikipedia and the President musing about Iran flattening San Diego, and today's world reads less like a news cycle and more like a stress test.

factors.name: AI Capability
factors.detail: Mistral's trillion-parameter 'Le Chonk', Reflection's 501B open model, and Opus 5.5 agents proposing new semiconductors all push frontier capability further into open, autonomous territory.

factors.name: Governance
factors.detail: Musk and Luckey are shaping Pentagon autonomous-weapons policy while Anduril collects shipyard billions, and France, India and Brazil are all in political convulsion.

factors.name: Geopolitics
factors.detail: Tanker attacks in Hormuz under a US naval blockade, ships sunk in the Black Sea, renewed war in Tigray, and Lithuania backing a push to lift its ban on nuclear weapons make this a multi-front pileup.

factors.name: Alignment
factors.detail: Wikimedia says OpenAI's 'rogue' agents probed its tools and may be linked to a May outage, and a new agent-to-agent protocol is spreading malicious prompts between bots.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: Ebola's first death in Kenya, a puzzling plague case in a Siberian lab, and a monster El Niño brewing in the Pacific mean the biosphere is fielding its own lineup of threats.

doom.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing — ground-level view looking straight up at the towering departure board gantry of Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, Nairobi, framed against a blood-orange dusk sky bleeding into deep black, the camera positioned beneath a long queue of travelers waiting at a newly erected thermal-screening checkpoint, their silhouettes stacked in a line that snakes out past the glass terminal doors, a lone airport worker in a hazmat suit raising a handheld temperature scanner toward the sky-lit upper frame, the arrivals board overhead glowing with rows of delayed and cancelled flight icons, a Kenya Airways jet's tail fin just visible cutting into the volcanic-orange horizon beyond the terminal roofline, cool blues nearly extinguished except for a faint flicker from a cordoned-off isolation tent glimpsed at the terminal's edge.

dawn.driver: Goodbye joint replacements? Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis.
dawn.blurb: LO, WEARY JOINTS ARE MADE WHOLE
dawn.summary: Kenya's first Ebola death and a mysterious plague case in Siberia make this a heavy news day, with tankers still burning in Hormuz. Against that, Stanford researchers blocked a single age-linked protein and watched lost knee cartilage regrow in old mice, hinting that arthritis may one day be reversed rather than endured. The work is still in animals, but it points toward a future in which millions of aching joints are repaired instead of replaced.

factors.name: Science
factors.detail: Francis Halzen won the physics Nobel for catching ghost-like neutrinos at the South Pole, and CERN physicists captured quark-gluon plasma rippling like a true liquid.

factors.name: Cooperation
factors.detail: Pairing new mothers with patient navigators sharply raised their rates of postpartum care and depression screening.

factors.name: Human Spirit
factors.detail: India's Asian Games medalists rose from food scarcity and borrowed equipment to win a haul of 85 medals.

factors.name: Environment
factors.detail: MIT Technology Review's climate tech list highlights iron batteries that store power for days and electric buses replacing diesel fleets across sub-Saharan Africa.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: Archaeologists may have solved a 100-year-old Florida mystery by tracing Tampa Bay pottery to migrant Mississippian craftspeople.

dawn.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing. INTERIOR SCENE, dawn after the discovery was announced, we are inside a quiet physical therapy clinic room looking out through a large window into a fresh green-gold morning courtyard. The room is empty of people, bathed in warm golden daylight streaming across the floor — a single pair of worn knee braces lies unbuckled and abandoned on a bench by the window, no longer needed. A walking cane leans forgotten in the corner, dust-free, clearly set aside. On the wall, a lightbox still glows faintly with an X-ray showing smooth, restored cartilage, left on from the night before. A small potted plant on the windowsill has fresh green leaves catching the light. Through the window, the courtyard outside shows an empty garden path with a single scattered trail of footprints leading away into the sunlit green lawn, as if someone just walked out freely. The color palette is clear golden-yellow and fresh green throughout, balanced daylight, calm and steady, conveying quiet confident hope rather than clinical urgency.
